problem: The 8086 half of the section treats the 8255 as if it had a full 8-bit address bus: it says A1 and A0 of the CPU go to the 8255 and that base 80H gives the block 80H-83H. On an 8086 the data bus is 16 bits wide, so the 8255 (a byte-wide device) sits on one byte lane only. If its D0-D7 connect to CPU D0-D7, CPU A0 cannot go to the 8255; the 8255's A0 and A1 must connect to CPU A1 and A2 (CPU A0 left unused or used to force even addresses). The registers then appear at 80H, 82H, 84H, 86H, not 80H-83H. The earlier generic statement in Section 1 is fine for an 8-bit bus; the 8086 paragraph is not.
fix: Write: on an 8086 the 8255 is a byte-wide peripheral on one byte lane. With the 8255 on D0-D7, connect 8255 A0 to CPU A1 and 8255 A1 to CPU A2; CPU A0 is not connected to the chip (it only selects the byte lane). Base 80H then gives port A at 80H, port B at 82H, port C at 84H, control at 86H; on the upper lane D8-D15 the same registers are at 81H, 83H, 85H, 87H. The decoder compares A3-A15 with the base, and for I/O-mapped access it must also qualify CS with M/IO low.

problem: "Mode 0 is simple input or output: the CPU reads or writes the port and the pin holds the level" suggests that input is latched, which it is not. Students then look for a latch on the input side.
fix: Say: in mode 0 an output pin is driven from a latch, so it holds the last byte written until the CPU writes again; an input pin is only buffered, not latched, so the CPU must read while the peripheral is still presenting the data.

problem: "One output can drive a few TTL inputs" is loose. The port pin sinks about 1.6-1.7 mA, which is roughly one standard TTL input (1.6 mA), not several. Several inputs are possible only with low-power Schottky (LS) TTL, which needs about 0.4 mA each.
fix: Say: one output drives one standard TTL input, or about four LS TTL inputs; for a whole board add a buffer or driver.

problem: "The CMOS 82C55 and pin-compatible GPIO expanders such as the MCP23017 over I2C" can be read as saying the MCP23017 is pin-compatible with the 8255, which it is not; only the 82C55 is pin-compatible.
fix: Rephrase: the CMOS 82C55 is pin-compatible with the 8255; register-based GPIO expanders such as the MCP23017 (over I2C) do the same job in a different package and bus.

problem: The data bus buffer node has no outgoing edge. The control word and port data travel from the buffer to the group A/B control blocks and to the ports on the internal data bus, but the diagram shows only the read/write logic driving the control blocks, so a student cannot see how the control word reaches the ports.
fix: Add edges from the data bus buffer to group A control, group B control, port A, port B and port C, labelled internal data bus, keeping the existing read/write logic and control-block edges.
